Sure, i made some assumptions about why he was asking. It was crappy answer even then. :-)

Well first you need to consider, this system has an external power source (garden hose) that's not found in nature anywhere. Earth is more of a low-pressure high-flow system than that: 40psi doesn't last for long in nature.

Second, what do you think hydroelectric dams do? We create a high pressure differential with a tall column of water, then draw from the bottom and use the pressure to turn a turbine. They're a little more optimized than that design, but the same basic principle is there.

As far as scaling up, I'd say that a dam is pretty damn large. The Hoover Dam is 726 feet tall, and a column of water that high generates 319psi of pressure at the bottom - more than enough to generate some power!

Yes in theory (if you mean the turbine itself, not the running it off mains water bit), but I think conventional turbine technology just advanced to the point where conventional turbines are easier and cheaper to use at scale.

Another option for a house that uses a lot of water and has good water pressure is stick one of these on their water intake to recover some of the energy from your mains water. Huh, that's actually not a bad idea...

Late Edit: Yes it is, the energy available is so trivial it's not worth the inconvenience to get it. 1 litre of water flowing at 1kPa gives 1kJ, so even if your tap water is at 10 bar and you use a kilolitre a day that's only 1MJ = 270 Wh.

Larger turbines are usually designed for energy efficiency above every other consideration. If I remember right, the Tesla turbine is not especially efficient, so it would not be chosen.

The Tesla turbine might find use in hydroelectric plants that need to be extremely simple, reliable, and easy to repair. If I were a scientist and wanted a water powered experimental station in a cave, I would put the Tesla turbine at the top of my list because it is so simple and clog resistant.
